title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 157 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 776–779 (Night 157, continuing directly from nights-156), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 157 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The slave-girl finishes her account: Shams al-Nahār swooned a second time at another song of parted lovers, and the caliph, knowing nothing of her passion, sat with her till morning and called in the physicians. Abū al-Ḥasan sends the girl back with advice to keep the secret, and at nightfall goes to ʿAlī, who begs him for help and to stay the night; ʿAlī recites two poems, the second a bravura kāmil piece on the beloved's glance, mole and teeth, then cries out and swoons until dawn. Next morning the slave-girl comes to the shop with a letter from Shams al-Nahār, and Abū al-Ḥasan leads her by a roundabout way to ʿAlī's house. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-seventh night,
sentences.n: al-sābiʿa, “the seventh”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَالَتْ لِأَبِي الْحَسَنِ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ سَيِّدَتِي هَذَا الشِّعْرَ وَقَعَتْ عَلَى الصُّفَّةِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jāriyata qālat li-Abī al-Ḥasani fa-lammā samiʿat sayyidatī hādhā al-shiʿra waqaʿat ʿalā al-ṣuffati maghshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the slave-girl said to Abū al-Ḥasan: And when my-lady heard this poetry, she-fell on the bench, swooned-upon.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the slave-girl said to Abū al-Ḥasan, “When my lady heard these verses, she fell down upon the dais in a swoon.
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together (السعيدان); the spacing is kept. al-jāriyata is accusative after anna. As each night opens, Shahrazād picks up the thread by repeating the last sentence of the night before: the slave-girl’s words here are those on which Night 156 closed. li-Abī al-Ḥasani: li-, “to”, marks the one spoken to, and abū, “father”, becomes abī after it. maghshiyyan ʿalayhā, “swooned upon”: the passive participle stays masculine, agreeing with the impersonal swoon, and ʿalayhā names the woman it came over; it is accusative, describing her state.

sentences.t: فَأَمْسَكْتُ يَدَهَا وَرَشَشْتُ عَلَي وَجْهِهَا مَاءَ الْوَرْدِ فَأَفَاقَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-amsaktu yadahā wa-rashashtu ʿalā wajhihā māʾa al-wardi fa-afāqat
sentences.l: And I-took-hold-of her-hand and sprinkled upon her-face water of the rose, and she-came-to.
sentences.i: I took her hand and sprinkled rose-water on her face, and she came to herself.
sentences.n: The print writes ʿalā, “upon”, with a final ي (علي), its usual swapping of ي and ى; it is pointed عَلَي and read ʿalā. māʾu al-wardi, “water of the rose”, is rose-water, the standard restorative for a swoon. afāqa, “to come to, recover one’s senses”, is form IV of a root meaning “to awaken”. The damma of فامسكتُ is the print’s own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدَتِي لَا تَهْتِكِي نَفْسَكِ وَمَنْ يَحْوِيهِ قَصْرُكِ فَبِحَيَاتِ مَحْبُوبِكِ أَنْ تَصْبِرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā yā sayyidatī lā tahtikī nafsaki wa-man yaḥwīhi qaṣruki fa-bi-ḥayāti maḥbūbiki an taṣbirī
sentences.l: And I-said to-her: O-my-lady, do-not tear-the-veil-of yourself and whoever your-palace contains-him; so by the-life-of your-beloved, that you-be-patient!
sentences.i: And I said to her, ‘My lady, do not bring shame on yourself and on everyone within your palace. By the life of your beloved, I beg you, be patient!’
sentences.n: The print runs the vocative yā into sayyidatī (ياسيدتي); the spacing is kept. lā tahtikī, “do not tear (the veil of)”: lā with the jussive is a prohibition, and the feminine -ī keeps its form while the nūn of the indicative drops. hataka, “to rend a veil”, is to expose someone’s secret to public shame; here the danger is that the caliph will learn of her love, ruining her and all her household. man yaḥwīhi qaṣruki, “whoever your palace contains (him)”: the -hi refers back to man, as Arabic relative clauses require. The print spells ḥayāt, “life”, with an open ت (حيات) rather than ة, as Middle Arabic often does with a word standing first in a construct. fa-bi-ḥayāti maḥbūbiki an taṣbirī, “by the life of your beloved, that you be patient”: bi- is the preposition of oath, “by”, and an with the subjunctive taṣbirī carries the entreaty, with the verb of begging (“I ask you”) left unsaid.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ هَلْ فِى الْأَمْرِ أَكْثَرُ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ فَأَنَا أَطْلُبُهُ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ فِيهِ رَاحَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat hal fī al-amri aktharu mina al-mawti fa-anā aṭlubuhu wa-Allāhi inna fīhi rāḥatī
sentences.l: And she-said: Is there in the matter more than death? Then I seek-it; by-God, indeed in-it (is) my-rest.
sentences.i: She answered, ‘Can anything come of this worse than death? Then death is what I seek, for by God, in death is my rest.’
sentences.n: hal, the particle of a yes-or-no question, here asks a question that expects no answer: nothing can be worse than death. fa-anā aṭlubuhu, “then I seek it”: the -hu is death. inna fīhi rāḥatī, “indeed in it is my rest”: after inna the subject, rāḥatī, comes after the prepositional phrase fīhi and stays accusative, though with the possessive -ī no ending shows. The print writes fī, “in”, here with ى (فى); a few words on, in the next sentence, it uses ي (في).

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ فِي هَذَا الْكَلَامِ إِذْ غَنَّتْ جَارِيَةٌ بِقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā naḥnu fī hādhā al-kalāmi idh ghannat jāriyatun bi-qawli al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And while we (were) in this speech, then sang a-slave-girl with the-saying of the poet:
sentences.i: And while we were talking so, a singing-girl sang these lines of the poet:
sentences.n: baynamā … idh, “while … then”: the stock frame for an interruption, the action under way in the first half and what breaks in upon it, opened by idh, in the second. ghannat bi-qawli al-shāʿiri, “sang with the saying of the poet”: ghannā takes bi- for the words sung; qawl al-shāʿir, “the poet’s saying”, is the usual way of announcing a quotation of verse. jāriyatun is indefinite: one of the caliph’s singing-girls, not the narrator.

sentences.t:
وَقَالُوا لَعَلَّ الصَّبْرَ يَعْقِبُ رَاحَةً * فَقُلْتُ وَاَيْنَ الصَّبْرُ بَعْدَ فِرَاقِهِ
وَقَدْ اَكَّدَ الْمِيثَاقَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُ * بِقَطْعِ حِبَالِ الصَّبْرِ عِنْدَ عِنَاقِهِ
sentences.tr:
wa-qālū laʿalla al-ṣabra yaʿqibu rāḥatan * fa-qultu wa-ayna al-ṣabru baʿda firāqihi
wa-qad akkada al-mīthāqa baynī wa-baynahu * bi-qaṭʿi ḥibāli al-ṣabri ʿinda ʿināqihi
sentences.l:
And they-said: Perhaps patience brings-after-it rest. * And I-said: And where is patience after his-parting?
And he-has made-firm the covenant between-me and between-him * by the-cutting of the-ropes of patience at his-embracing.
sentences.i:
They said, ‘Perhaps patience will bring rest in its wake.’ I said, ‘And where is patience, now that he is gone?
He sealed the covenant between us when we embraced, by cutting through the ropes of patience.’
sentences.n: The print has اصبر, a misprint for الصبر, corrected here. The rest of the pointing is the print’s own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of وَاَيْنَ and اَكَّدَ, where the edition marks no hamza. laʿalla, “perhaps”, takes its subject, al-ṣabra, in the accusative. The print points yaʿqibu with a fatḥa on the prefix, as if from the simple verb ʿaqaba, “to follow”; the sense wanted, “to bring in its wake”, is the form IV aʿqaba, yuʿqibu, and the print’s vowel is probably a slip; either reading scans. The second line is the conceit: the beloved bound the lover with a covenant whose seal was the severing of every rope of patience, so that patience is the one thing he cannot have. ʿinda ʿināqihi, “at his embracing”: the embrace of parting.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنَ الشِّعْرِ وَقَعَتْ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat mina al-shiʿri waqaʿat maghshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And when she-finished from the poetry, she-fell, swooned-upon.
sentences.i: When the singer had finished her verses, my lady fell down in a swoon.
sentences.n: The two feminine verbs have different subjects, and neither is named: the singer, who faraghat min, “finished with”, her song, and Shams al-Nahār, who waqaʿat, “fell”. The hearer is left to sort them out by the sense. maghshiyyan ʿalayhā, “swooned upon”, as before: the passive participle stays masculine, and ʿalayhā names the one the swoon came over.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَهَا الْخَلِيفَةُ فَأَتَى مُسْرِعًا إِلَيْهَا وَأَمَرَ بِرَفْعِ الشَّرَابِ وَأَنْ تَعُودَ كُلُّ جَارِيَةٍ إِلَى مَقْصُورَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarahā al-khalīfatu fa-atā musriʿan ilayhā wa-amara bi-rafʿi al-sharābi wa-an taʿūda kullu jāriyatin ilā maqṣūratihā
sentences.l: And the caliph saw-her, and he-came hastening to-her, and he-ordered the lifting-away of the drink, and that every slave-girl return to her-chamber.
sentences.i: The caliph saw her and came hurrying to her side, and he ordered the wine to be cleared away and every slave-girl to go back to her own apartment.
sentences.n: naẓarahā, “he saw her”, with a direct object: Classical says naẓara ilayhā, “looked at her”, and the transitive use is the later language. musriʿan, “hastening”, is an accusative participle describing how he came. amara bi-, “to order”: the verb chooses bi- for the thing commanded, here the noun rafʿ, “lifting, removal”; the second thing commanded is given as a clause, an taʿūda, “that she return”, subjunctive after an, and both hang on the one amara. maqṣūra, “a closed-off room”, is a private apartment in the palace.

sentences.t: وَأَقَامَ عِنْدَهَا بَاقِيَ لَيْلَتِهِ إِلَى أَنْ أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ
sentences.tr: wa-aqāma ʿindahā bāqiya laylatihi ilā an aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu
sentences.l: And he-stayed with-her the remainder of his-night, until the morning came-to-morning.
sentences.i: He stayed with her the rest of the night, until morning came.
sentences.n: bāqiya laylatihi, “the remainder of his night”, is an accusative of time. aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, the stock phrase again; ilā an with a past verb is “until”.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَدْعَى أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِالْحُكَمَاءِ وَالْأَطِبَّاءِ وَأَمَرَهُمْ بِمُعَالَجَتِهَا وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِمَا هِيَ فِيهِ مِنَ الْعِشْقِ وَالْغَرَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-istadʿā amīru al-muʾminīna bi-al-ḥukamāʾi wa-al-aṭibbāʾi wa-amarahum bi-muʿālajatihā wa-lam yaʿlam bi-mā hiya fīhi mina al-ʿishqi wa-al-gharāmi
sentences.l: And the Commander of the Faithful called for the wise-men and the physicians, and he-ordered-them to her-treating; and he-did-not know of what she (was) in-it of the passion and the love-longing.
sentences.i: Then the Commander of the Faithful sent for the sages and the physicians and ordered them to treat her, knowing nothing of the passion and love-sickness that held her.
sentences.n: istadʿā bi-, “to call for, summon”: bi- marks who is sent for. amara bi-, “to order”, again with bi- for the thing ordered, here muʿālaja, “treatment”, the verbal noun of form III ʿālaja, with -hā, “her”, as its object. ʿalima bi-, “to know of”: the verb chooses bi-. bi-mā hiya fīhi, “of what she was in”, i.e. the state she was in, and min al-ʿishqi wa-al-gharāmi spells out what that was: min here explains the vague mā. ʿishq is passionate love; gharām, love as a torment that will not let go. The hamza of المؤمنين is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهَا حَتَّى ظَنَنْتُ أَنَّهُ قَدِ انْصَلَحَ حَالُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-aqamtu ʿindahā ḥattā ẓanantu annahu qadi inṣalaḥa ḥāluhā
sentences.l: And I-stayed with-her until I-thought that it — her-state had-already mended.
sentences.i: I stayed with her until I thought she was on the mend.
sentences.n: The slave-girl now speaks of herself again: aqamtu, “I stayed”. annahu, “that it”, carries an empty pronoun, the “it” of the matter, and the clause that follows says what the matter is. inṣalaḥa, “to come right, be mended”, is form VII of ṣalaḥa: a later formation, where Classical says ṣalaḥa or ṣaluḥa itself. Its verb is masculine with ḥāl, “state”, as the print usually treats that noun.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي عَاقَنِي عَنِ الْمَجِيءِ إِلَيْكُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā huwa alladhī ʿāqanī ʿani al-majīʾi ilaykumā
sentences.l: And this, it (is) that-which held-me-back from the coming to-you-two.
sentences.i: That is what kept me from coming to you both.
sentences.n: huwa, “it”, the separating pronoun between subject and predicate, marks alladhī … as the predicate: “this is the thing that …”. ʿāqa ʿan, “to hinder from”. The dual -kumā, “you two”, is Abū al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī. The hamza of المجيء is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ تَرَكْتُ عِنْدَهَا جَمَاعَةً مِنْ خَوَاصِّهَا مُشْتَغِلِينَ الْقَلْبَ عَلَيْهَا لَمَّا أَمَرَتْنِي بِالْمَسِيرِ إِلَيْكُمَا لِآخُذَ خَبَرَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَأَعُودَ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad taraktu ʿindahā jamāʿatan min khawāṣṣihā mushtaghilīna al-qalba ʿalayhā lammā amaratnī bi-al-masīri ilaykumā li-ākhudha khabara ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-aʿūda ilayhā
sentences.l: And I-have-left with-her a-group of her-intimates, busied the heart over-her, when she-ordered-me to the going to-you-two, so-that I-take the news of ʿAlī son of Bakkār and return to-her.
sentences.i: I left a number of her closest attendants with her, their hearts full of worry for her, when she ordered me to go to you both to fetch news of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and come back to her.”
sentences.n: khawāṣṣ, “intimates”, the plural of khāṣṣa, those closest to her, here her own women. mushtaghilīna al-qalba ʿalayhā, “busied of heart over her”: an accusative describing them, with al-qalba, “the heart”, saying in what respect they are busied; Classical would rather say mushtaghilī al-qalbi or mushtaghilatan qulūbuhum. The participle is masculine plural though the attendants are women, the later language's general plural. amara bi-, “to order”, with bi- for the thing ordered, masīr, “going”. li-ākhudha, “so that I take”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, and aʿūda shares it. akhadha khabaran, “to take news”, to get word of someone. The shadda of لمّا and the madda of لآخذ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ كَلَامَهَا تَعَجَّبَ وَقَالَ لَهَا وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي أَخْبَرْتُكِ بِجَمِيعِ خَبَرِةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Abū al-Ḥasani kalāmahā taʿajjaba wa-qāla lahā wa-Allāhi innī akhbartuki bi-jamīʿi khabarihi
sentences.l: And when Abū al-Ḥasan heard her-speech, he-wondered, and he-said to-her: By-God, indeed-I have-informed-you of all his-news.
sentences.i: When Abū al-Ḥasan heard what she said he was astonished, and he said to her, “By God, I have told you everything about him.
sentences.n: The print runs Abū al-Ḥasan together here (ابوالحسن); it is kept and pointed as one word. wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of the oath, with the genitive. akhbara … bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news. He has already told her all of ʿAlī's state before she began her own story, and now says so. The print spells the pronoun of khabarihi, “his news”, with ة (خبرة); the letters are kept and read by the sense.

sentences.t: فَعُودِي إِلَى سَيِّدَتِكِ وَسَلِّمِي عَلَيْهَا وَبَالِغِي لَهَا فِى الصَّبْرِ وَحُثِّيهَا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿūdī ilā sayyidatiki wa-sallimī ʿalayhā wa-bālighī lahā fī al-ṣabri wa-ḥuththīhā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: So return to your-lady, and give-greeting upon-her, and go-to-lengths for-her in the patience, and urge-her to-it,
sentences.i: Go back to your lady, give her my greetings, press her hard to be patient and urge her to it,
sentences.n: The imperatives are feminine singular, -ī, addressed to the slave-girl. sallimī ʿalayhā, “greet her”: sallama ʿalā, to give someone the salām. bālighī lahā fī al-ṣabri, “go to lengths for her in patience”: bālagha fī, form III, is to do a thing to the utmost, here to press patience on her as hard as she can; li- marks the one it is done for. ḥaththa ʿalā, “to urge to”: ʿalā marks what she is urged to, and ʿalayhi, “to it”, is patience. The shaddas of وسلّمي and وحثّيها are the print's own; the print writes fī as فى.

sentences.t: وَقُولِي لَهَا اُكْتُمِي السِّرَّ وَأَخْبِرِيهَا أَنِّي عَرَفْتُ أَمْرَهَا وَهُوَ أَمْرٌ صَعْبٌ يَحْتَاجُ إِلَى التَّدْبِيرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qūlī lahā uktumī al-sirra wa-akhbirīhā annī ʿaraftu amrahā wa-huwa amrun ṣaʿbun yaḥtāju ilā al-tadbīri
sentences.l: and say to-her: Hide the secret; and inform-her that I have-known her-affair, and it (is) a-hard affair, needing the managing.
sentences.i: and tell her, ‘Keep the secret.’ And let her know that I understand her situation, and that it is a hard one that wants careful handling.”
sentences.n: The print has آكتمي, with a stray madda, a misprint for اكتمي, corrected here. uktumī, “hide, keep”, is the feminine imperative of katama, its alif read u- because the stem vowel is u; the slave-girl is to pass it on to her lady. akhbirīhā, “inform her”, form IV imperative with -hā as its object. wa-huwa amrun ṣaʿbun, “and it is a hard affair”, is a circumstantial clause opened by wa-. iḥtāja ilā, “to need”: ilā marks what is needed. tadbīr, “management, contriving”, is form II of dabbara, to think a matter through to its end. The shadda of السرّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَشَكَرَتْهُ الْجَارِيَةُ وَوَدَّعَتْهُ وَانْصَرَفَتْ إِلَى سَيِّدَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-shakarathu al-jāriyatu wa-waddaʿathu wa-inṣarafat ilā sayyidatihā
sentences.l: And the slave-girl thanked-him, and bade-him-farewell, and went-off to her-lady.
sentences.i: The slave-girl thanked him, took her leave, and went back to her lady.
sentences.n: inṣarafa, “to turn away, depart”, form VII of ṣarafa. The shadda of وودّعته is the print's own.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهَا وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ أَبِى الْحَسَنِ فَإِنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ فِي دُكَّانِهِ إِلَى آخِرِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihā wa-ammā mā kāna min amri Abī al-Ḥasani fa-innahu lam yazal fī dukkānihi ilā ākhiri al-nahāri
sentences.l: This (is) what was of her-affair; and as-for what was of the affair of Abū al-Ḥasan, then indeed-he did-not cease in his-shop until the end of the day.
sentences.i: So much for her. As for Abū al-Ḥasan, he stayed in his shop until the end of the day.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna min amrihā … wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what there was of her affair … and as for what there was of the affair of …”: the Nights' stock formula for leaving one character and taking up another. ammā is answered by fa-, here fa-innahu. lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with fī: he stayed on. The print writes Abī as ابى, with final ى; the madda of آخر is its own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا مَضَى النَّهَارُ قَامَ وَعَزَلَ دُكَّانَهُ وَقَفَلَ وَأَتَى إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ فَدَقَّ الْبَابَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā maḍā al-nahāru qāma wa-ʿazala dukkānahu wa-qafala wa-atā ilā dāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin fa-daqqa al-bāba
sentences.l: And when the day passed, he-rose and cleared his-shop and locked-up, and came to the house of ʿAlī son of Bakkār and knocked-on the door.
sentences.i: When the day was over he got up, shut up his shop and locked it, and went to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār's house and knocked at the door.
sentences.n: ʿazala, “to set aside, remove”, is used of a shop for clearing in the wares and closing for the day, a later usage. qafala, “to lock”, here without an object: “he locked up”. daqqa al-bāba, “he knocked at the door”, with the door as the direct object.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ لَهُ بَعْضُ غِلْمَانِهِ وَأَدْخَلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja lahu baʿḍu ghilmānihi wa-adkhalahu
sentences.l: And there-came-out to-him one-of his-pages and brought-him-in.
sentences.i: One of ʿAlī's servants came out to him and showed him in.
sentences.n: baʿḍu ghilmānihi, “some of his pages”, i.e. one of them: baʿḍ with a plural often means a single one. ghilmān, plural of ghulām, “boy”, is young male servants. The pronoun of ghilmānihi is ʿAlī's. adkhala, “to make enter”, form IV of dakhala.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ تَبَسَّمَ وَاسْتَبْشَرَ بِقُدُومِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhala ʿalayhi tabassama wa-istabshara bi-qudūmihi
sentences.l: And when he-entered upon-him, he-smiled and rejoiced at his-coming.
sentences.i: When he came in to ʿAlī, ʿAlī smiled, delighted that he had come.
sentences.n: Again the subjects shift without being named: Abū al-Ḥasan enters, ʿAlī smiles. istabshara bi-, “to rejoice at”, form X of the root of bushrā, “good news”: the verb chooses bi- for what gladdens. qudūm, “arrival”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَبَا الْحَسَنِ أَوْحَشْتَنِي لِتَخَلُّفِكَ عَنِّي فِي هَذَا الْيَوْمِ وَرُوحِي مُرْتَهَنَةٌ بِكَ بَاقِيَ عُمْرِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu yā Abā al-Ḥasani awḥashtanī li-takhallufika ʿannī fī hādhā al-yawmi wa-rūḥī murtahanatun bika bāqiya ʿumrī
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: O Abū al-Ḥasan, you-made-me-desolate by-your-staying-behind from-me on this day; and my-soul (is) pledged to-you the remainder of my-life.
sentences.i: And he said, “Abū al-Ḥasan, how I have missed you, with you staying away from me all day! My soul is in pledge to you for the rest of my life.”
sentences.n: After yā the name takes the accusative, Abā. awḥashtanī, “you made me desolate”, form IV of the root of waḥsha, loneliness: the everyday way of saying “I missed you”. li-takhallufika, “because of your staying behind”: li- of cause, with takhalluf ʿan, “to stay away from”. murtahana bi-, “held in pledge by”: bi- marks the one who holds the pledge. rūḥ, “soul”, is feminine here, hence murtahanatun. bāqiya ʿumrī, “the rest of my life”, an accusative of time. The shadda of لتخلّفك is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ دَعْ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani daʿ hādhā al-kalāma
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: Leave this talk.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan answered, “Say no more of that.
sentences.n: daʿ, “leave”, is the imperative of wadaʿa, which has no past in use (taraka serves instead). The print again runs Abū al-Ḥasan together (ابوالحسن).

sentences.t: فَلَوْ كَانَ شِفَاؤُكَ بِيَدِي لَجُدْتُ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَسْأَلَنِي وَلَوْ أَمْكَنَ فِدَاكَ كُنْتُ أَفْدِيكَ بِرُوحِي
sentences.tr: fa-law kāna shifāʾuka bi-yadī la-judtu bihi qabla an tasʾalanī wa-law amkana fidāka kuntu afdīka bi-rūḥī
sentences.l: For if your-healing were in-my-hand, I-would-have-given-freely of-it before that you-ask-me; and if your-ransoming were-possible, I-was ransoming-you with-my-soul.
sentences.i: If your cure were in my hands, I would have given it before you ever asked; and if you could be ransomed, I would ransom you with my own life.
sentences.n: law … la-, “if … then would”: the first conditional has the Classical shape, with la- on the answer, judtu. jāda bi-, “to give generously”: the verb chooses bi- for what is given. bi-yadī, “in my hand”: bi- of place, “in my power”. qabla an tasʾalanī, “before you ask me”, subjunctive after an. The second conditional answers law with kuntu afdīka, “I was ransoming you”, kāna with an imperfect and no la-, the later language's way of saying “I would”. fidā, “ransom” (also fidāʾ), here fidāka, “your ransom”; fadā bi-, “to ransom with”: bi- marks the price. The hamzas of شفاؤك and تسألني are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَفِي هَذَا الْيَوْمِ جَاءَتْ جَارِيَةُ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَأَخْبَرَتْنِي أَنَّهُ مَا عَاقَهَا عَنِ الْمَجِيءِ إِلَّا جُلُوسُ الْخَلِيفَةِ عِنْدَ سَيِّدَتِهَا وَأَخْبَرَتْنِي بِمَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ سَيِّدَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-fī hādhā al-yawmi jāʾat jāriyatu Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-akhbaratnī annahu mā ʿāqahā ʿani al-majīʾi illā julūsu al-khalīfati ʿinda sayyidatihā wa-akhbaratnī bi-mā kāna min amri sayyidatihā
sentences.l: And on this day the slave-girl of Shams al-Nahār came and informed-me that it (is): nothing held-her-back from the coming except the sitting of the caliph with her-lady; and she-informed-me of what was of the affair of her-lady.
sentences.i: Today Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl came and told me that the only thing that had kept her from coming was the caliph's sitting with her lady; and she told me all that had happened to her lady.”
sentences.n: annahu, “that it”, with the empty pronoun of the matter, as above. mā … illā, “nothing … except”: the negation with illā singles out julūs al-khalīfati as the one hindrance. akhbara … bi-mā, “told of what”: bi- marks the news. The hamzas of جاءت and المجيء and the shadda of الّا are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَحَكَى لَهُ جَمِيعَ مَا سَمِعَهُ مِنَ الْجَارِيَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥakā lahu jamīʿa mā samiʿahu mina al-jāriyati
sentences.l: And he-related to-him all of what he-heard-it from the slave-girl.
sentences.i: And he told him everything he had heard from the slave-girl.
sentences.n: ḥakā, “to relate, tell over”, with li- for the listener. mā samiʿahu, “what he heard it”: the -hu takes up mā, a resumptive pronoun Arabic uses freely after a relative.

sentences.t: فَتَأَسَّفَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ غَايَةَ الْأَسَفِ وَبَكَي ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى أَبِى الْحَسَنِ وَقَالَ لَهُ بِاللّٰهِ عَلَيْكَ يَا أَخِي أَنْ تُسَاعِدَنِي فِيمَا بُلِيتُ بِهِ وَعَلِّمْنِي كَيْفَ تَكُونُ الْحِيلَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-taʾassafa ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin ghāyata al-asafi wa-bakā thumma iltafata ilā Abī al-Ḥasani wa-qāla lahu bi-Allāhi ʿalayka yā akhī an tusāʿidanī fīmā bulītu bihi wa-ʿallimnī kayfa takūnu al-ḥīlatu
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār grieved the utmost of grief, and wept; then he-turned to Abū al-Ḥasan and said to-him: By God (I-lay-it) upon-you, O my-brother, that you-help-me in what I-have-been-afflicted with, and teach-me how the way-out may-be.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār grieved to the utmost and wept; then he turned to Abū al-Ḥasan and said, “By God, my brother, I beg you to stand by me in this trial that has come upon me, and teach me what can be done.”
sentences.n: taʾassafa, form V of asifa, “to grieve, be sorry”; ghāyata al-asafi, “the utmost of grief”, is an accusative standing in for the verbal noun: he grieved with the utmost grief. The print spells bakā with dotted yāʾ (وبكي), as it often does with final-weak verbs; a little further on it writes وبكى. Abī al-Ḥasani: abū becomes abī after the preposition ilā, and the print writes it with final ى (ابى). bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God, upon you”, is an adjuration, “I adjure you by God”, and what is asked follows as an an-clause with the subjunctive tusāʿidanī. bulītu, “I have been afflicted”, passive of balā, “to try, test”; bihi, “with it”, points back to mā, “what”. ʿallimnī, “teach me”, imperative of form II ʿallama. kayfa takūnu al-ḥīlatu, “how the device is to be”: ḥīla is a stratagem or way out of a difficulty.

sentences.t: وَأَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ أَنْ تَبِيتَ عِنْدِي هَذِةِ اللَّيْلَةَ لِأَسْتَأْنِسَ بِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-asʾaluka min faḍlika an tabīta ʿindī hādhihi al-laylata li-astaʾnisa bika
sentences.l: And I-ask-you of your-bounty that you-spend-the-night with-me this night, that I-may-take-comfort in-you.
sentences.i: And I ask you, of your kindness, to spend this night with me, so that I may take comfort in your company.
sentences.n: min faḍlika, “of your bounty”, is the courteous “please”. an tabīta, “that you spend the night”: subjunctive after an; bāta is used only of the night. hādhihi al-laylata is an accusative of time; the print spells hādhihi with ة (هذة), as is its habit. li-astaʾnisa, “so that I may find comfort”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive; istaʾnasa bi-, form X of anisa, “to find company and solace in someone”, bi- marking the companion. The hamza of اسألك (after its first alif) and of لاستأنس is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَامْتَثَلَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ أَمْرَةُ وَأَجَابَهُ عَلَى الْمَبِيتِ عِنْدَةُ فَبَاتَا يَتَحَادَثَانِ فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-imtathala Abū al-Ḥasani amrahu wa-ajābahu ʿalā al-mabīti ʿindahu fa-bātā yataḥādathāni fī tilka al-laylati
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan complied-with his-command, and answered-him (yes) to the staying-the-night with-him; and the-two passed-the-night talking-with-each-other in that night.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan did as he asked and agreed to stay the night with him, and the two of them spent that night talking together.
sentences.n: The print runs abū and al-ḥasan into one word (ابوالحسن); the spacing is kept. It spells the pronoun -hu with ة in امرة (amrahu, “his command”) and عندة (ʿindahu, “with him”), its habit, though in اجابه the same pronoun is spelled ه. imtathala amrahu, “he complied with his command”, form VIII of mathala. ajābahu ʿalā al-mabīti, “he answered him (yes) to staying the night”: ajāba ʿalā is to consent to; mabīt is the verbal noun of bāta. bātā, “the two of them spent the night”, is dual, and the dual imperfect yataḥādathāni, form VI, “talking with one another”, says how they spent it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ اللَّيْلُ تَأَوَّهَ عَلِيُّ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَبَكَى وَاشْتَكَى ثُمَّ أَرْسَلَ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā janna al-laylu taʾawwaha ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-bakā wa-ishtakā thumma arsala al-ʿabarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And when the night grew-dark, ʿAlī son of Bakkār sighed, and wept, and complained; then he-let-loose the tears and recited these verses:
sentences.i: When night had fallen, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār sighed and wept and lamented; then he let his tears flow and recited these verses:
sentences.n: janna al-laylu, “the night grew dark”: janna is “to cover, conceal”, the root of jinn and of janna, “garden”. taʾawwaha, form V, “to say āh”, to sigh in pain. ishtakā, form VIII of shakā, “to complain”. arsala al-ʿabarāti, “he sent forth the tears”: ʿabarāt is the plural of ʿabra, “tear”, and as a feminine sound plural its accusative ends in -i. Here the print writes bakā with ى (وبكى), and again writes ibn with its alif (ابن) between the two names. It spells hādhihi with ة (هذة). abyāt, plural of bayt, “line of verse”. The hamza of تأوه is the print's own.

sentences.t:
خَيَالُكَ فِيْ عَيْنِيْ وَذِكْرُكَ فِيْ فَمِيْ * وَمَثْوَاكَ فِيْ قَلْبِيْ فَكَيْفَ تَغِيْبُ
وَمَا اَسَفِيْ اِلَّا عَلَى الْعُمْرِ يَنْقَضِيْ * وَلَيْسَ لَنَا فِى الْاِجْتِمَاعِ نَصِيْبُ
sentences.tr:
khayāluka fī ʿaynī wa-dhikruka fī famī * wa-mathwāka fī qalbī fa-kayfa taghību
wa-mā asafī illā ʿalā al-ʿumri yanqaḍī * wa-laysa lanā fī al-ijtimāʿi naṣību
sentences.l:
Your-image (is) in my-eye, and your-remembrance in my-mouth, * and your-dwelling-place in my-heart: so how do-you-go-absent?
And my-grief is not except over the life passing-away, * while there-is-not for-us in the being-together a-share.
sentences.i:
Your image is in my eye, your name upon my lips, your dwelling in my heart: how then can you be absent?
My only grief is for life that runs out, while we have no share in being together.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the sukūn it sets on long vowels (فِيْ, عَيْنِيْ) and the bare alif of اَسَفِيْ and اِلَّا, where the edition marks no hamza. It also points the alif after the article in الْاِجْتِمَاعِ with a kasra, though in reading that alif is silent: fī al-ijtimāʿi. The print writes fī as فِى in line 2. The metre is ṭawīl, rhyming in -bu. In line 1 khayāl is the image of the absent beloved that the eye keeps seeing; dhikr, “remembrance”, is in the mouth because the name is always on the lips; mathwā is “abode, place of staying”. In line 2 mā … illā, “not … except”, means “only”; yanqaḍī, “passing away”, is a circumstantial clause on al-ʿumr, “life”, and wa-laysa lanā …, “while we have no …”, is another. naṣīb, “share, portion”, is the subject of laysa, held back to the end for the rhyme.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And the saying of the other:
sentences.i: And the words of another poet:
sentences.n: A heading for the next poem, in the nominative with its predicate left unsaid: “and (here is) the saying of the other”, al-ākhar being another poet. The madda of الآخر is the print's own.

sentences.t:
خَفَرَتْ بِسَيْفِ اللَّحْظِ ذِمَّةَ مِغْفَرِيْ * وَفَرَتْ بِرُمْحِ الْقَدِّ دِرْعَ تَصَبُّرِيْ
وَجَلَتْ لَنَا مِنْ تَحْتِ مِسْكَةِ خَالِهَا * كَافُوْرَ فَجْرٍ شَقَّ لَيْلَ الْعَنْبَرِ
فَزَعَتْ فَضَرَّسَتِ الْعَقِيْقَ بِلُؤْلُؤٍ * سَكَنَتْ فَرَائِدُهُ غَدِيْرَ السُّكَّرِ
وَتَنَهَّدَتْ جَزَعًا فَاَثَّرَ كَفُّهَا * فِيْ صَدْرِهَا فَنَظَرْتُ مَالَمْ اَنْظُرِ
اَقْلَامَ مَرْجَانٍ كَتَبْنَ بِعَنْبَرٍ * بِصَحِيْفَةِ الْبَلُّوْرِ خَمْسَةَ اَسْطُرَ
يَاحَامِلَ السَّيْفِ الصَّحِيْحِ اِذَا رَنَتْ * اِيَّاكَ ضَرْبَةَ جَفْنِهَا الْمُتَكَسِّرِ
وَتَوَقَّ يَارَبَّ الْقَنَاةِ الطَّعْنَ اِنْ * حَمَلَتْ عَلَيْكَ مِنَ الْقِوَامِ بِاَسْمَرِ
sentences.tr:
khafarat bi-sayfi al-laḥẓi dhimmata mighfarī * wa-farat bi-rumḥi al-qaddi dirʿa taṣabburī
wa-jalat lanā min taḥti miskati khālihā * kāfūra fajrin shaqqa layla al-ʿanbari
fazaʿat fa-ḍarrasati al-ʿaqīqa bi-luʾluʾin * sakanat farāʾiduhu ghadīra al-sukkari
wa-tanahhadat jazaʿan fa-aththara kaffuhā * fī ṣadrihā fa-naẓartu mā lam anẓuri
aqlāma marjānin katabna bi-ʿanbarin * bi-ṣaḥīfati al-ballūri khamsata asṭura
yā ḥāmila al-sayfi al-ṣaḥīḥi idhā ranat * iyyāka ḍarbata jafnihā al-mutakassiri
wa-tawaqqa yā rabba al-qanāti al-ṭaʿna in * ḥamalat ʿalayka mina al-qiwāmi bi-asmari
sentences.l:
She-violated, with the sword of the glance, the protection of my-helmet, * and she-split, with the spear of the stature, the mail-coat of my-endurance.
And she-unveiled for-us, from beneath the musk of her-mole, * a camphor of dawn that split the night of the ambergris.
She-took-fright, and bit the carnelian with a-pearl * whose single-pearls dwell-in a pool of the sugar.
And she-sighed in-anguish, and her-palm left-marks * on her-breast; and I-saw what I-had-not seen:
pens of coral that-wrote with ambergris, * on the page of the crystal, five lines.
O bearer of the sound sword, when she-gazes, * beware the blow of her-eyelid, the broken-one!
And guard-against, O master of the lance, the thrust, if * she-charges against-you, of the stature, with a tawny-one!
sentences.i:
With the sword of her glance she broke the safe-conduct of my helmet, and with the spear of her figure split the mail of my endurance.
From beneath the musk of her mole she unveiled to us a camphor dawn that split a night of ambergris.
Startled, she bit into carnelian with pearls whose single gems lie in a pool of sugar.
She sighed in her distress, and her palm left its traces on her breast, and I saw what I had never seen:
pens of coral that had written in ambergris five lines upon a page of crystal.
You who carry a sword unbroken, when she turns her gaze on you, beware the stroke of her languid eyelid;
and you who bear a lance, guard against the thrust, if she charges at you with the tawny spear of her slender form.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of فَاَثَّرَ, اَنْظُرِ, اَقْلَامَ, اَسْطُرَ, اِذَا, اِيَّاكَ, اِنْ and بِاَسْمَرِ, where the edition marks no hamza; the hamzas of لُؤْلُؤٍ and فَرَائِدُهُ are the print's too. The print runs mā lam (مَالَمْ) and the vocative yā with the noun after it (يَاحَامِلَ, يَارَبَّ) into single words; the spacing is kept. The metre is kāmil, rhyming in -ri. The poem arms the beloved and disarms the lover. Line 1 plays khafarat against mighfar, “helmet”: khafara is “to protect”, but with a pledge of protection (dhimma) as object it can also mean “to break” it, the sense more often carried by akhfara, and breaking is what the line wants; farat is from farā, “to cut, split”; her glance is the sword, her straight, slender figure (qadd) the spear. Line 2: jalat, from jalā, “to unveil”; the dark mole is musk, her face a camphor-white dawn breaking through the ambergris-dark night of her hair. Line 3: the print points fazaʿat with fatḥa on the zāy, where the usual form is faziʿat; it is kept. ḍarrasa, form II, “to bite hard”; the carnelian is her lips, the pearl her teeth, farāʾid, “single large pearls”, the separate teeth, and the pool of sugar her sweet mouth; ghadīra is the direct object of sakanat, “dwelt in”. Line 4: kaff, “palm”, is usually feminine, but its verb aththara, “left marks”, is masculine, as a verb that comes first may be with a noun not female by sex. Line 5 explains mā lam anẓuri and is in the accusative after naẓartu: her hennaed fingertips are coral pens that wrote five lines in ambergris on the crystal page of her breast; bi-ʿanbarin, “with ambergris”, bi- of the instrument, and bi-ṣaḥīfati, “on the page”, bi- of place. The print points اَسْطُرَ with fatḥa; after khamsata the genitive (asṭurin, in rhyme asṭuri) is expected, and the rhyme wants -ri, so the fatḥa is doubtful; it is kept and translated as “lines”. Line 6 turns on jafn, which means both “eyelid” and “scabbard”, and sets ṣaḥīḥ, “sound, unbroken”, against mutakassir, “broken”, here the languid, drooping eye; idhā ranat, “when she gazes”; iyyāka with an accusative, “beware of”. Line 7: tawaqqa, imperative of form V tawaqqā, “guard yourself against”; rabb al-qanāt, “master of the lance”; ḥamala ʿalā, “to charge at”, with bi- of the weapon; asmar, “tawny”, is a stock word both for a spear and for a slender brown figure, and mina al-qiwāmi, “of the stature”, says which is meant; it is a diptote, here given -ri for the rhyme. The print points qiwām with kasra, where the word for “stature” is usually qawām. The line runs on: in, “if”, closes the first half and its verb ḥamalat opens the second.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ مِنْ شِعْرِةِ صَرَخَ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً وَوَقَعَ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin min shiʿrihi ṣarakha ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan wa-waqaʿa maghshiyyan ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār finished from his-poetry, he-shrieked a-shriek great, and fell swooned-upon.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār had finished his verses, he gave a great cry and fell down in a swoon.
sentences.n: The print spells the pronoun with ة: شعرة is shiʿrihi, “his poetry”. faragha min, “to be done with”. ṣarakha ṣarkhatan, “shrieked a shriek”: the verb takes its own noun as an object (the cognate accusative), and the adjective ʿaẓīmatan carries the weight. maghshiyyan ʿalayhi, “swooned upon”: the passive participle is accusative, describing his state as he falls.

sentences.t: فَظَنَّ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ أَنَّ رُوحَهُ خَرَجَتْ مِنْ جَسَدِةِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ فِي غَشْيَتِهِ حَتَّى طَلَعَ النَّهَارُ فَأَفَاقَ وَتَحَدَّثَ مَعَ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ
sentences.tr: fa-ẓanna Abū al-Ḥasani anna rūḥahu kharajat min jasadihi wa-lam yazal fī ghashyatihi ḥattā ṭalaʿa al-nahāru fa-afāqa wa-taḥaddatha maʿa Abī al-Ḥasani
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan supposed that his-soul had-gone-out from his-body; and he-did-not cease in his-swoon until the day rose, and he-came-to and talked with Abū al-Ḥasan.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan thought his soul had left his body; but he lay in his swoon until daybreak, when he came to himself and talked with Abū al-Ḥasan.
sentences.n: The print spells the pronoun with ة: جسدة is jasadihi, “his body”. rūḥ, “soul”, is here feminine (kharajat); it is used in both genders. The subject changes without being named: Abū al-Ḥasan supposes, but it is ʿAlī who stays in his swoon and then revives. lam yazal, “he did not cease”: lam with the jussive negates the past, and lam yazal is “he remained, went on”. afāqa, “to come to, revive” (Form IV).

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ جَالِسًا عِنْدَةُ إِلَى ضَحْوَةِ النَّهَارِ فَقَامَ وَانْصَرَفَ مِنْ عِنْدِةِ وَجَاءَ إِلَى دُكَّانِهِ وَفَتَحَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal Abū al-Ḥasani jālisan ʿindahu ilā ḍaḥwati al-nahāri fa-qāma wa-inṣarafa min ʿindihi wa-jāʾa ilā dukkānihi wa-fataḥahā
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan did-not cease sitting with-him until the forenoon of the day; then he-rose and turned-away from beside-him, and came to his-shop and opened-it.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan stayed sitting with him until the morning was well on; then he rose and left him, and went to his shop and opened it.
sentences.n: The print runs Abū and al-Ḥasan together (ابوالحسن); the spacing is kept. It also spells the pronoun with ة twice: عندة is ʿindahu, “with him”, after jālisan, and ʿindihi, “from beside him”, after min. lam yazal … jālisan, “did not cease sitting”: the participle in the accusative gives what he went on doing. ḍaḥwat al-nahār, “the forenoon of the day”, the bright part of the morning before midday. As in the last night, dukkān, “shop”, takes a feminine pronoun (fataḥahā).

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْجَارِيَةِ قَدْ جَاءَتْهُ وَوَقَفَتْ عِنْدَةُ فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ إِلَيْهَا أَوْمَأَتْ إِلَيْهِ بِالسَّلَامِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهَا السَّلَامَ وَبَلَّغَتْهُ سَلَامَ سَيِّدَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-jāriyati qad jāʾathu wa-waqafat ʿindahu fa-lammā naẓara ilayhā awmaʾat ilayhi bi-al-salāmi fa-radda ʿalayhā al-salāma wa-ballaghathu salāma sayyidatihā
sentences.l: And behold, the slave-girl had come-to-him and stood with-him; and when he looked at-her she-signed to-him with the greeting, and he-returned upon-her the greeting, and she-conveyed-to-him the greeting of her-lady.
sentences.i: And there was the slave-girl, come to him and standing by him. When he looked at her she made him a sign of greeting; he returned it, and she gave him her lady's greeting.
sentences.n: The print spells the pronoun with ة: عندة is ʿindahu. wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: idhā of surprise, with bi- only marking what appears. awmaʾa ilā, “to make a sign to” (Form IV): she greets him by a gesture, bi-al-salām naming what the sign conveyed, as befits a message carried in secret. radda ʿalayhā al-salāma, “he returned the greeting to her”: ʿalā marks the one greeted, as in sallama ʿalā. ballagha, “to convey” (Form II), takes two objects, the person (-hu) and the thing conveyed (salāma). The hamza of اومأت and the shaddas of فردّ and وبلّغته are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ كَيْفَ حَالُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu kayfa ḥālu ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: How (is) the state of ʿAlī son of Bakkār?
sentences.i: And she asked him, “How is ʿAlī ibn Bakkār?”
sentences.n: kayfa ḥālu …, “how is the state of …”: a sentence with no verb, the usual way of asking after someone.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَا جَارِيَةَ الْخَيْرِ لَا تَسْأَلِي عَنْ حَالِهِ وَمَا هُوَ فِيهِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْغَرَامِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَنَامُ اللَّيْلَ وَلَا يَسْتَرِيحُ بِالنَّهَارِ وَقَدْ أَنْحَلَهُ السَّهَرُ وَغَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ الضَّجَرُ وَصَارَ فِي حَالٍ لَا يَسُرُّ حَبِيبًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā jāriyata al-khayri lā tasʾalī ʿan ḥālihi wa-mā huwa fīhi min shiddati al-gharāmi fa-innahu lā yanāmu al-layla wa-lā yastarīḥu bi-al-nahāri wa-qad anḥalahu al-saharu wa-ghalaba ʿalayhi al-ḍajaru wa-ṣāra fī ḥālin lā yasurru ḥabīban
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: O girl of the good, do-not ask about his-state and what he (is) in-it of the intensity of passion; for indeed-he does-not sleep the night and does-not rest by the day; and wakefulness has wasted-him, and weariness has prevailed over-him, and he-has-become in a-state (that) does-not gladden a-friend.
sentences.i: He said to her, “Good girl, do not ask how he is, nor what the violence of his passion has brought him to. He does not sleep at night nor rest by day; sleeplessness has worn him thin and weariness has mastered him, and he is in a state that would grieve anyone who loved him.”
sentences.n: yā jāriyata al-khayri, “O girl of goodness”: a kindly form of address; a vocative in construct takes the accusative. lā tasʾalī, “do not ask”: lā with the jussive is a prohibition, and the feminine tasʾalīna loses its nūn; the hamza of تسألي is the print's own. wa-mā huwa fīhi, “and what he is in”: mā is “that which”, and fīhi points back to it. min shiddati al-gharāmi explains the mā: “by way of the violence of passion”. bi-al-nahāri, “by day”: bi- of time. anḥalahu al-saharu, “sleeplessness has made him thin”: anḥala, Form IV of naḥala, “to grow thin”; the object pronoun comes before the subject. lā yasurru ḥabīban, “that does not gladden a friend”: a clause describing the indefinite ḥālin without a relative word, and a stock phrase for a sorry state. ḥāl, “state”, is masculine here (yasurru); it is used in both genders.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ سَيِّدَتِي تُسَلِّمُ عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَيْهِ وَقَدْ كَتَبَتْ لَهُ وَرَقَةً وَهِيَ فِي حَالٍ أَعْظَمَ مِنْ حَالِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu inna sayyidatī tusallimu ʿalayka wa-ʿalayhi wa-qad katabat lahu waraqatan wa-hiya fī ḥālin aʿẓama min ḥālihi
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: Indeed my-lady greets upon-you and upon-him; and she-has written to-him a-paper, and she (is) in a-state greater than his-state.
sentences.i: She said to him, “My lady sends her greetings to you and to him. She has written him a letter, and she is in a worse way than he is.”
sentences.n: sallama ʿalā, “to greet” (Form II): the verb chooses ʿalā for the one greeted. waraqa, “a sheet of paper”, here a letter. wa-hiya fī ḥālin …, “she being in a state …”: wa- with a pronoun opens a circumstantial clause. aʿẓama min, “greater than”: an elative with min is a comparative; aʿẓam is diptote, so its genitive ends in -a. “Greater” here means graver: her plight is worse than his.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سَلَّمَتْنِي الْوَرَقَةَ وَقَالَتْ لَا تَأْتِينِي إِلَّا بِجَوَابِهَا وَافْعَلِي مَا أَمَرْتُكِ بِهِ وَهَا هِيَ الْوَرَقَةُ مَعِي فَهَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تَسِيرَ مَعِي إِلَيْهِ وَنَأْخُذَ مِنْهُ الْجَوَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad sallamatnī al-waraqata wa-qālat lā taʾtīnī illā bi-jawābihā wa-ifʿalī mā amartuki bihi wa-hā hiya al-waraqatu maʿī fa-hal laka an tasīra maʿī ilayhi wa-naʾkhudha minhu al-jawāba
sentences.l: And she-has handed-me the paper and said: Do-not come-to-me except with its-answer, and do what I-commanded-you with-it. And here she (is), the paper, with-me; so is (it) for-you that you-go with-me to-him and we-take from-him the answer?
sentences.i: “She has handed me the letter and said, ‘Do not come back to me without the answer; and do as I have told you.’ Here is the letter with me now. Will you come with me to him, so that we can get the answer from him?”
sentences.n: sallama, “to hand over” (Form II), takes two objects, the person (-nī) and the thing (al-waraqata). lā taʾtīnī illā bi-jawābihā, “do not come to me except with its answer”, i.e. come back only with the reply: atā bi- is “to bring”, the verb choosing the preposition; lā with the jussive is a prohibition, and the feminine taʾtī (from taʾtīna, nūn dropped) takes the object -nī. The print writes تاتيني with a bare alif and no hamza; the hamza is supplied. The -hā of jawābihā is the letter (waraqa is feminine). amara bi-, “to command”: bihi marks what is commanded. wa-hā hiya al-waraqatu, “and here it is, the letter”: hā, “behold”, with the pronoun pointing ahead. fa-hal laka an …, “is it for you that …”, a polite “would you be willing to …”; tasīra and naʾkhudha are both subjunctive after an. The shadda of الّا and the hamza of ونأخذ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَبُوالْحَسَنِ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Abū al-Ḥasani samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-her: hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan answered her, “Hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: ابوالحسن is again printed as one word. samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan: two accusatives standing for a verb left unsaid, the stock formula of compliance.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَفَلَ الدُّكَّانَ وَأَخَذَ مَعَهُ الْجَارِيَةَ وَذَهَبَ بِهَا مِنْ مَكَانٍ غَيْرِ الَّذِي جَاءَ مِنْهُ وَلَمْ يَزَالَا سَائِرَيْنِ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَا إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ ثُمَّ أَوْقَفَهَا عَلَى الْبَابِ وَدَخَلَ
sentences.tr: thumma qafala al-dukkāna wa-akhadha maʿahu al-jāriyata wa-dhahaba bihā min makānin ghayri alladhī jāʾa minhu wa-lam yazālā sāʾirayni ilā an waṣalā ilā dāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin thumma awqafahā ʿalā al-bābi wa-dakhala
sentences.l: Then he-locked the shop and took with-him the slave-girl, and went with-her from a-place other than the-one he-came from-it; and the-two did-not cease travelling until they-two arrived at the house of ʿAlī son of Bakkār. Then he-stood-her at the door and went-in.
sentences.i: Then he locked up his shop and took the slave-girl with him, leading her by a different way from the one she had come by, and the two of them walked on until they reached the house of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār. There he left her standing at the door and went in.
sentences.n: dhahaba bi-, “to go with”, i.e. to take someone along. min makānin ghayri alladhī jāʾa minhu, “from a place other than the one he came from”: ghayr agrees as a genitive with makānin, and minhu is the resumptive pronoun the relative clause needs. Whose coming is meant is not plain: jāʾa is masculine, so strictly Abū al-Ḥasan's, but the sense is the girl's road, a different way so that the two are not seen together. lam yazālā sāʾirayni, “the two did not cease travelling”: the dual jussive drops its nūn. The print's سائرين can be read as dual or plural; the dual fits the two of them, and its hamza is the print's own. ilā an waṣalā, “until they arrived”. awqafa, “to make stand, stop” (Form IV): he left her waiting at the door.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
